en: The Scripture on the Buddha-Nature, the Ocean-Treasury, Wisdom, Liberation, and the Shattering of Mental Characteristics.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, between a pair of *śāla* trees on the bank of the [Hiraṇyavatī] River.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, he was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*.
Together with a multitude of eighty billion gods and humans who were free from calamity,
they all gathered at the Buddha’s dwelling,
wailing and sobbing with grief.
The great earth shook violently,
and springs and sources boiled and surged,
like a compassionate mother who has just lost her beloved child.
Tears filled his eyes;
he could not restrain himself and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
It was like the collapse of Mount Sumeru;
blood flowed from each and every pore,
drenching the ground like *pārijātaka* flowers.
How painful! How bitter!
The world is now empty and void;
our unsurpassed compassionate father has, in a single moment, abandoned us and entered into parinirvāṇa.
We are solitary and destitute; upon whom shall we rely?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and pity.
Furthermore, remain in the world and do not enter parinirvāṇa;
for the sake of my disciples, widely proclaim and disseminate the unsurpassed medicine of the Dharma,
so that sentient beings of future generations may leave suffering behind and transcend the world.
"We shall hear it, uphold it, practice it,
and widely proclaim and disseminate it everywhere so that it never ceases.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Cease, all of you!
Do not speak such words.
Those who were to be delivered by my appearance in this world have now all been delivered."
That which was to be spoken has now been fully expounded.
At midnight, he entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, there was a mahāsattva within the assembly.
The Dharma Prince named Removing Doubt rose from his seat,
adjusted his robes, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, I observe that the Tathāgata’s wisdom, eloquence, and supernormal powers are unimpeded and immeasurable, and his skillful means are like space.
Why then do you say,
"That which was to be said has already been said"?
Having finished speaking these words,
the entire great assembly raised their voices in loud wailing, their grief shaking heaven and earth,
as blood flowed from their eyes.
"Are we, your followers, not indeed your children?
Thus they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground like corpses.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
Out of compassion for the great assembly, he spoke these words to dispel their doubts:
"Excellent! You are a Great Being who, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas..."
He made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
he was fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation,
and he felt compassion for all sentient beings.
It is well that you are able to pose such a question.
Listen attentively, listen attentively,
and all you in the great assembly, reflect upon this well.
"I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Excellent, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.
"Good son," [the Buddha replied].

All sentient beings are enveloped by signs; whether they depart from doubt or are released from their bonds, it is all due to awakening to the fundamental principle (*zong*), whereby both sign and [conceptualization] are simultaneously lost—this is called the School of Emptiness (*kongzong*).
In the Prajñā, emptiness and existence coexist.
They are called followers of the Two Vehicles;
clinging to signs and contravening the fundamental tenets,
they are termed Śrāvakas.
Ordinary beings spend their entire lives within the three realms with no prospect of escape;
they undergo all manner of suffering and have not yet attained liberation.
This is truly because one has been struck by the arrows of the three poisons,
bitten by the four snakes,
and plundered by the five dogs.
It is that which is terrified by the six thieves,
submerged by the seven killers,
and dragged away by the eight heterodoxies.
A cluster of myriad evils;
transmigrating through birth and death,
coming and going among the six realms of existence.
They surge forth into the five realms of rebirth,
falling into the three miserable paths and the eight difficulties,
where there is never a moment of happiness.
It is called the Avīci Great Hell.
Enveloped by afflictions, various evils compete to arise,
ultimately forming knots of enmity.
The sun of wisdom has suddenly faded its brilliance;
the light of compassion is gradually vanishing.
We are thus lost upon the true path.
"How truly pitiable!
At that time, the Great Being Vimatisudāna addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One, what are called the three poisonous arrows?"
"Is its shape and size visible?
I only wish for you to explain this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the monk Vimatisamudghātin, saying:
Regarding the three poisonous arrows:
they are neither with signs nor without signs.
Having had his doubts removed, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, why do you say it is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics?
If it were not with characteristics,
then that which is not a source of affliction would not be a source of affliction.
How is it that what can be named is called an arrow?
If it were not signless (animitta), it would be visible;
because it is visible, it should also be avoidable.
How is it that they are able to harm sentient beings?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and conditions so that all may hear and know them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Mahāsattva Dispeller of Doubts:
"You now possess immeasurable great compassion and take pity upon those suffering from their transgressions;
you desire to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation, knowledge, vision, and unimpeded wisdom."
He is now able, within this great assembly, to reveal the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
having attained benefit for himself, he further benefits all sentient beings.
You members of the great assembly, listen attentively with silent mindfulness.
I shall proclaim for you the essential points of the Dharma.
Noble son, as for the arrows of the three poisons:
It is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because the five aggregates exist, it is called "not non-existent";
because the five aggregates are empty, it is called "not existent."
It is ignorance and craving that constitute this.
Since worldly things cannot be obtained,
one falsely gives rise to a mind of grasping.
This is called delusion.
These were originally one's own possessions,
yet they have been abandoned and departed.
To give rise to vain recollections is called craving;
it is the greedy attachment to female form.
This is called desire.
Because these three types of mind arise in a state of confusion, one is termed an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
For those in hell, deluded mind is the fermenting agent.
The heart of love is the rice.
When the rice and the yeast are mixed together, they produce the wine of desire.
Because one is intoxicated by drinking this wine, one fails to recognize one's father, mother, or brothers, and proceeds to kill them all.
This is called "harm," because due to a lack of compassion,
it severs the lineage of the Three Jewels.
The discrimination of grasping and rejecting between self and others is called the five pungent vegetables;
because of their foul odor,
they defile the field of the sentient beings' bodies.
"The waters of my wisdom have long been obstructed and have not emerged;
therefore, it is said that we do not dwell in the same country nor drink from the same river. What you have done is not the same as mine."
It is that very mind which, of its own accord,
considers itself to have produced something subtle and excellent, surpassing others, and thinks, "This is my mind."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not something heard; to give rise to false hearing and receiving is the mind of grasping.
Phenomena are without movement; to give rise to false transmigration is the mind of relinquishing.
The nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, lacking any essence; to give rise to false signs of difference is discrimination.
For this reason, they are called "deluded sons";
they do not attain transcendence from the world and are thus termed "conditioned sentient beings of the mundane realm."
When these words were spoken,
the entire assembly accepted them in silence with faith. Good son.
The deluded mind is the seed;
the mind of craving is the soil.
The seed enters the soil.
As rain about to fall pours down, the root of ignorance arises from this very source.
To practice the Path without removing delusion and craving is like felling a tree without removing its roots.
It is called a stump;
branches and twigs grow from the stump,
eventually becoming a great tree.
The foolish people of the world are likewise so.
All afflictions arise from the causes of ignorance and craving,
and thus give rise to self-conceit and doubt.
The darkness of ignorance is vast;
it thus forms the three obstructions, a dwelling place dug out by nescience.
This is precisely what that refers to.
At that time, the Mahāsattva Remover of Doubts,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
rose from his seat.
He adjusted his robes and addressed the great assembly:
"From time immemorial, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas..."
Having heard these phrases from Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
he upheld and practiced them without ever becoming weary or indolent.
Now, having again heard the aforementioned chapters and verses,
my mind is filled with joy;
I have attained an unprecedented method.

Only then did he come to know that the Great Sage Tathāgata, with the light of wisdom, extensively gives rise to the Dharma-gate within the three realms of existence to receive in his embrace all his children;
he causes demons and heretics to return to the truth,
and as the six masters gradually vanish, he employs skillful means to construct twelve Dharma-ships to rescue those in peril and distress.
I cause them all to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi,
so that they may ascend the path to the eightfold noble way and nirvana.
Yet all sentient beings are ignorant and deluded, believing in what is false and turning their backs on what is correct.
To grasp the truth by relying on the words while remaining estranged from the meaning of its nature is merely laborious and useless,
like a single wheel of a chariot.
How could one possibly rely upon such [views]?
They may merely share the same sounds and harmonize their outward expressions, yet they have not realized the true reality (tattva).
Such individuals as these are truly to be pitied.
How painful! How bitter!
What can repentance avail now?
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Excellent! It is just as you have said;

it is true and not false. At that time, the Great Being Vimatisamudghātin, having received the Buddha’s seal of approval, immediately praised and questioned him in the midst of the assembly with these verses:
I contemplate the Tathāgata’s truly wondrous body, Pure and stainless like a lotus flower;
His wisdom and skillful means are equal to space, His liberation is unimpeded, able to open and close,
His sovereign spiritual powers are boundless, Beholding all equally without partiality.
I now prostrate to the Greatly Wise and Luminous One; I pray that you enter the signless meaning of empty stillness.
I only wish that you would explain it through skillful means for me, So that my doubts may be removed and I may attain awakening.
The true nature of phenomena, the single reality so difficult to know— Pray manifest your form for me, so that I may know its locus.

"Out of compassion for us, your deluded children, you have extensively analyzed and expounded the profound and true meaning for the sake of the great assembly; you have thundered the great Dharma-thunder for my sake.
At that time, the World-Honored One—
Then, wishing to restate this meaning for the great assembly,
he spoke these verses:
"Sentient beings within the three realms Are constantly bound by the five aggregates, Transmigrating through the three states of existence."

Failing to attain the bliss of liberation, one undergoes new suffering for billions of eons; because of possessing the body of the five aggregates, one does not behold the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).
This is called a person in birth-and-death (saṃsāra), whose mind is constantly pierced by the three poisons and heated like a blazing fire;
finding no peace anywhere, they are entangled by the mutual characteristics of the afflictions (kleśa).
Wandering back and forth through the five realms, how can one describe such sorrow? The three miserable paths serve as my dwelling;
shackles and fetters bind my body. Due to these arrows of the three poisons, my wisdom-body is harmed;
I lack mastery over my own coming and going—how then can I see the Truth? A deluded mind serves as the fermenting agent.
Affectionate love is its rice; delusion and craving are combined with it. Those who drink become intoxicated and cannot awaken, remaining unenlightened through vast eons.
Because of this wine of the three poisons, they are bewildered and lose the right path, sinking and clinging within the three realms of existence.
Their own minds are perpetually dark and disordered; they have not yet vomited up the turbid wine.
Failing to meet a virtuous friend, one runs wild and mad through the darkness. Seeing the Buddha, one fails to recognize the Real and gives rise to the defilement of pride.
The discriminating mind is impure; it is because of drinking the wine of ignorance that the deluded mind becomes a seed of darkness.
The mind of attachment serves as the soil of confusion; thus, darkness and delusion encounter one another.
From this collection of afflictions, ignorance arises as the root; all [afflictions] rain down through craving and form branches in an instant.
To extinguish them, one must use the axe of wisdom. If one cuts down a tree but does not remove the root, the nature of the tree remains and its source is not exhausted;
from the root, branches grow, and flowers and fruits flourish ever more profusely.
The various views are its seeds; arrogance is its walls and fences. Clinging to false appearances while protecting the true self, it is swallowed by ignorance.
The three poisons are its root, and the afflictions are likewise so.
When the stumps and stumps are entirely removed, it is called a fertile field, where the sprouts of Bodhi can grow.
Because there are no roots or stumps, The arrows of the three poisons are uprooted. The body attains a state of stability;
The yeast of delusion is not employed, And the grain of craving is cast away upon the ground.
Since the wine of desire is no longer produced, One will surely attain great, luminous wisdom. When the mind is empty and its characteristics exhausted, Wisdom and contemplative cultivation arise.
The two emptinesses are signless; The body dwells within a radiant pavilion. Blazing like a mass of fire, its light opens the gates of hell.
Unimpeded and inconceivable, The response-body becomes a Tathāgata.
My original practice was thus; Now I have escaped the three calamities And dwell securely in the Immovable Ground.
"Verified as the most excellent for humans and devas, you should practice this with diligence.
In the future, we shall certainly meet again, and you will attain perfect enlightenment just as I have, without any difference.
At that time, the Mahāsattva Dispeller of Doubts addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Bhagavān, how is it that sentient beings in this world are bitten by four venomous snakes?
What is their appearance such that they may be recognized?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me,
so that those who lack eyes may be encouraged to overcome this difficulty.
The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is malice, anger, and envy.
World-Honored One, what state of mind is this malice, anger, and envy?"
Yet it is named a snake.
The Buddha said:
"It does not depend on what others deem good."
When it festers within, it is called an abscess;
when anger does not issue forth from the mouth,
it is called resentment.
Fearing that others may surpass oneself is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
Seeing the goodness of others and not obstructing their excellence is [the opposite].
This is called envy.
These four poisonous snakes dwell within the well of the mind;
they gnaw through the roots of goodness, causing one to faint and die.
They fall into the three miserable realms and undergo great suffering.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these words, he immediately entered samādhi.
Emerging from samādhi, he emitted a great radiance.
It universally illuminated the trichiliocosm,
and the entire great assembly beheld the radiance.
With one voice and in unison, they addressed the Mahāsattva Dispeller of Doubts, saying:
The light emitted by the World-Honored One was different from his usual radiance;
whereas on previous occasions when he emitted light,
it first illuminated the eastern direction.
Today light is emitted,
illuminating the ten directions simultaneously from all four sides.
By what causes and conditions has such an auspicious omen appeared?
"I only pray that the Benevolent One will explain this for me.
At that time, the Mahāsattva Dispeller of Doubts addressed the great assembly:
"I have heard that the Tathāgata’s light of wisdom, throughout the long night, should be identical with the three realms of existence."
He utters the medicine of the Dharma from his mouth to heal the myriad ailments of sentient beings,
thereby causing their suffering to cease forever;
even the venomous snakes hide within their holes.
The true path of delusion and awakening eradicates birth and death;
the three miserable realms are transformed into the palace of nirvāṇa,
and the darkness of ignorance is changed into the great illumination of the seed of omniscience.
Transform malice into loving-kindness;
transform anger into compassion;
cultivate envy into sympathetic joy.
Transforming envy into equanimity,
one immediately accomplishes the four immeasurable minds;
this is called the gateway of wisdom.
It is also called the Well of Wisdom.
One should know that this light is precisely the illumination of the Tathāgata’s great compassion and wisdom;
the gates of hell open so that sentient beings who have lost their way may follow the light and attain happiness.
I have heard that when the Tathāgata first taught the ninefold canon,
he spoke of conditioned merits as being like a master diviner who surveys the ground and digs a well,
yet does not yet know whether the water will be sweet or bitter.
It is the same for all sentient beings:
if they perceive the Buddha-nature, it is called sweet water;
if they do not realize the principle of emptiness, it is called bitter water.
To exert effort with equal strength yet labor as if it were useless—
such is the case for the śrāvaka.
A person practicing the Way is like one digging a well.
Gradually the earth is removed;
when the earth is exhausted, the water naturally appears.
Sentient beings are also like this.
When the afflictions of the five aggregates are eliminated and exhausted,
the Buddha-nature emerges spontaneously.
Although one has obtained sweet water, there is no well of skillful means.
Without bricks to support it, it will inevitably be overwhelmed by sand and soil;
before long, the water will be completely exhausted,
and it shall be known as a dried-up well.
The followers of external paths are likewise so.
However, although all śrāvakas and beginner bodhisattvas have attained the removal of emptiness, it is not extensive.
To study various sutras without skillful means,
being oppressed by afflictions, is called the view of emptiness;
the retinue of Māra is likewise so.
By the power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s concentration of mind,
they employ unimpeded skillful means to create a well;
when water is accumulated therein, it becomes clear and pure, which is named the water of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Being inexhaustible, it is called the water of wisdom;
it can wash away the defilements of the mind,
so that the myriad delusions are thereby exhausted.
One cannot be harmed by any evils;
one cannot be defiled by afflictions or the cycle of birth and death.
For these reasons, it is named the Ocean of Sarvajñā (All-Knowledge).
It is also called the Ocean of Wisdom.
Just as a sea does not tolerate corpses,
this is exactly like that.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Mahāsattva Dispeller of Doubts:
"You have well understood my intention.
After my parinirvāṇa, you shall be among the great assembly."
He is able to bestow the eye upon others, extensively saving those who are blind;
he heals all manner of illnesses and sustains the life-force of wisdom for humanity.
In a future age, you shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment in Jambudvīpa,

receiving the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, known as the King of the Dharma of Radiance.
At that time, when you appear in the world,
the earth will be entirely pure and free from all impurities and evils;
food will be provided spontaneously, and there will be no suffering or affliction.
The hells find rest;
the hungry ghosts are satiated;
all is mild and harmonious.
The sequence of the four seasons is as follows:
the animals change their forms and there is neither male nor female;
the ground is level and even, utterly devoid of sand or soil.
The household furnishings were made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, pearls, and precious gems;
they were pure and unadulterated,
and he moved about with complete mastery.
It is like space:
vast and without rival.
Those who see this sutra and receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or circulate it shall all encounter your appearance in the world and attain great peace and happiness.
Therefore, you should receive, uphold, and disseminate this throughout the world so that it shall not be severed.
Why is this? Because upon hearing this sutra even once, one will not fall into the three miserable realms until the attainment of Buddhahood; for this reason, the evil paths will diminish.
If there are those who see or hear this and practice as taught—
with diligence, patience, and the observance of precepts without slackening—
they too shall become Buddhas after you.
"You should widely proclaim and disseminate this sutra wherever you go.
Its power is inconceivable;
wherever it reaches, malignant diseases shall be cured."
If one receives and maintains this with a sincere heart, there is no request that will not be fulfilled:
the mute shall speak, the lame shall walk, the blind shall see, and the deaf shall hear;
their physical faculties shall be complete, and they shall move through all places without obstruction.
Possessing eloquence and many capabilities,
the seven treasures fill [the realm] to overflowing,
and its radiance is brilliant and majestic.
Transcending the world, he is extraordinary and unique;
his glory and nobility are spontaneous,
and in his joy there is no sorrow or distress.
This sutra contains the most supreme and unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma;
those who seek a son shall obtain a son,
and those who seek a daughter shall obtain a daughter.
If one reveres and believes with a sincere heart, nothing will fail to accord with one's wishes;
yet if there are those who disparage it without faith,
or who lack reverence, [the result shall be otherwise].
To handle this sutra with impure hands;
to slander it and engage in contentious debate;
and to treat it with frivolous jesting and irrelevant metaphors through meaningless speech.
Such a person will, in their present life, suffer from blindness or physical deformities;
or they may be mute, deaf, or have a blocked nose.
They will be separated from their father and son, and driven away to wander in foreign lands.
They live by their labor, being employed by others;
impoverished and exhausted, they are terrified everywhere.
Having endured suffering, their lives come to an end.
They shall fall into the Black Darkness Hell for eight million years.
Only after emerging from there will they constantly be born into lowly and base circumstances;
for five hundred lifetimes, they shall not even hear the names of the Triple Gem.
After this person’s life has ended, they shall receive the body of a fish for ten great kalpas. Therefore,
you should skillfully employ expedient means and provide illustrative analogies.
Do not cause them to slander [the Dharma]. Speak it for the wise;
do not bestow it upon the foolish, for the foolish hear it and cannot understand.
They will inevitably give rise to slander;
they will undergo great suffering in the present life and,
upon death, enter the evil destinies.
"You have lost your compassion and thus cannot be called a Great Being.
At that time, the Great Being Dispeller of Doubts, for the sake of the great assembly and his own person,
desired to resolve their doubts once again.
He questioned the Buddha in verse:
As I contemplate the body of the Tathāgata, It is as pure as space. His eloquence and wisdom are unimpeded;
All who behold him pay him reverence. His skillful means and wisdom are immeasurable; He is able to sustain the lives of all beings.
All in my assembly are filled with doubt; I pray that you will explain the ultimate truth. Having already heard of the four poisons, how can one be free from this illness?
Please analyze this for me in detail, so that those who are deluded may awaken.
These four poisons are precisely the mind; how can they be eliminated? If one does not eliminate this mind, [how can there be liberation]?
The World-Honored One spoke of the illness of the mind: "The fundamental mind is not dual;
How can one further create a prior mind, a subsequent mind, and a middle mind? How can these various minds be eliminated?
If one mind gives rise to a second and a third, they suddenly arrive; Such mental objects are as vast as space."
"The World-Honored One has sent me to eliminate [doubts], yet I do not know how to eliminate them.
Out of compassion for the great assembly, you must surely speak for me. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Being Dispeller of Doubt, saying:
"Good son, you are a great being who takes pity on sentient beings of future generations."
Having asked this question,
you should listen attentively,
and you and the great assembly should reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain this for you.
Son of good family,
if one practices ten dharmas while wandering through the three realms, then the four poisons will not exist.
Question:
What are the ten?
The Buddha said:
First, their mind neither increases nor decreases in response to praise or blame.
Second, they maintain constant equanimity toward sentient beings of superior, middling, and inferior capacities.
Third, they give rise to great compassion for all, whether foolish or wise.
Fourth, regarding offerings from those who treat one with contempt or honor, the mind remains without duality.
Fifth, upon seeing the good or hearing of evil, the mind remains free from discrimination.
Sixth, when seeing others suffer loss or deficiency, one does not look for their faults.
Seventh, seeing that the various vehicles are all the One Vehicle.
Eighth, hearing of the sufferings of the three evil realms without being startled or terrified.
Ninth, regarding all sentient beings as the Tathāgata.
Tenth, because the Buddha appears among sentient beings and creates a sense of the marvelous,
it is said that the mind is so effusive as to be difficult to restrain,
like the playful antics of a monkey.
The six sense faculties universally take all objects as their conditions;
for this reason, the mind is distracted and not tranquil, like turbulent waves.
Within the three realms, they undergo birth and death.
Restrain the mind so that it is not negligent,
like a monkey bound by chains;
fix the mind upon a single point.
It can open the gate of wisdom. Good son,
the four poisonous minds are like water.
The body is like a wall;
as water gradually seeps into it,
the wall collapses.
Sentient beings are likewise;
the four poisons reside within their hearts,
gradually soaking them.
The body is subject to decay;
because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to relinquish it, they attain the eternally abiding body. Good son!
The four venomous snakes are likened to fire;
the body is likened to grass;
and the practitioner is likened to one who mows the grass.
Those who uphold the five precepts without deficiency obtain a human body;
those who mow grass without omission will surely harvest much grass.
Sentient beings are likewise.
If one cultivates goodness without laziness, one will surely attain rebirth among humans or devas.
When a great fire breaks out,
it burns away heaps of grass.
In the space of a mere finger-snap, everything is lost without remainder;
so it is for all practitioners as well when the four poisonous fires of evil break out.
It burns away the life-force of my wisdom,
causing it all to be utterly extinguished;
for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to remain far removed from it.
The wisdom-dharmakāya is eternally abiding and never extinguished.
Good son, what you have just asked has precisely captured its true meaning.
The answer I have now given does not miss its proper time;
it benefits immeasurable sentient beings and elucidates the Way and its teachings.
He delivers all the blind masses,
causing them to emerge from the three realms of existence and reach the further shore.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, [spoke as follows].
And he spoke in verse:
I contemplate the three realms as existing, yet they are dark, silent, and utterly formless. Arising and ceasing are like bubbles on water;
the bubbles and the water are fundamentally not two. If the water is unmoving, the substance of the bubbles does not manifest at all.
The bubble appears and then vanishes again; it is fundamentally no different from the water. The Buddha-nature is like space:
because of space, there is the appearance of existence. Because of the water, there is the appearance of the bubble. The essence of the bubble is emptiness;
though there is existence, existence and non-existence are not two distinct forms. The water and the bubble are neither one nor two; when the bubble appears, it manifests as two forms.
Bubbles submerge and return to oneness; where there is mind, there is body.

Emptiness and existence are non-dual when there is no mind, yet they are not one when the mind is fully present. The body has birth, and with the presence of mind, throughout kalpas it is never the same.
When the mind exists, the myriad phenomena respond; when phenomena respond, there is indulgence and dissipation.
From this, lust is born; through this, the four poisons arise. Amidst the delusions of the *mīḷha* (filth), one wanders like waves in darkness.
For this reason, one cannot be free from the notion of a self (*ātman*).
Now I shall explain for you: you must surely eliminate the impurities of the aggregates (*skandha*). Once these aggregate-impurities are exhausted, [liberation is attained].
The various defilements are not called "existence" (*bhava*); existence has its substance because of the body. This is called the defilement of all existences;
where there is defilement, there is the emptiness of signs. That which is empty has existence as its substance.
Because existence and non-existence are one, one and two can be absent. Because space is unimpeded, it should manifest in immeasurable forms.
No-mind is called a bodhisattva; having mind is called a sentient being.

On the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Baoying era of the Great Tang, the Śramaṇa Changhui of Yanxing Temple in the Central Capital, having been invited to provide offerings at Saiting to the west of Dunhuang City, unexpectedly encountered this scripture. As it lacked its beginning and title, and was incomplete, he subsequently obtained the upper scroll from the Zhibai Fotu to the east of Songqu and combined them into one volume. Fearing that later generations might not understand, he has recorded these inconceivable matters at the end of the text. May the merit of this compilation be extended to all; may we and all sentient beings together attain the Buddha-way.
